paper.title: Explore, Select, Derive, and Recall: Augmenting LLM with Human-like Memory for Mobile Task Automation
paper.central_claim: An LLM mobile task automator with a human-like hierarchical app memory (explore-select-derive-recall) can automate and learn new tasks with 82.7% accuracy, adapt learned tasks to new parameters with near-perfect (98.75%) accuracy, and cut latency and cost by 62.5% and 68.8% versus a same-prompt GPT-4 baseline.
paper.title_note: Material text is titled 'MobileGPT: Augmenting LLM with Human-like App Memory for Mobile Task Automation' (v3); manifest title is the earlier arXiv variant. Same arXiv ID and version.

provenance.notes: actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref are not exposed to the worker agent; model_type follows the claude-kimi type overlay (haiku slot -> claude-sonnet-5-5[1m]) as dispatched by the controller.

rationale: 留存的任务/子任务/动作记忆使重复任务成本延迟大降(-62.5%/-68.8%)，但无人工修复的暖启动成功率(82.2%)不高于冷启动；98.75%含人工修复；单次运行无方差，自建数据集。

missing_sections: Figures 1-7 (workflow, repair UI, graph, bar charts) not rendered in text extraction; numbers used from prose/tables only. Prompts are not reproduced in the material.

evidence.quote: The results indicate that MobileGPT can automate and learn new tasks with 82.7% accuracy, and is able to adapt them to different contexts with near perfect (98.75%) accuracy while reducing both latency and cost by 62.5% and 68.8%, respectively, compared to the GPT-4 powered baseline.
evidence.support_explanation: Headline claims; note 98.75% and the 62.5/68.8% figures come from the ablation setting (Sec 7.3), not from the comparative Table 1.

evidence.quote: MobileGPT organizes its memory in the form of a transition graph that encapsulates the following key information:
evidence.support_explanation: Per-app graph of page nodes, sub-task edges (action sequences) and tasks as sequences of (node, sub-task).

evidence.quote: After MobileGPT successfully completes the user instruction, it stores the task as a collection of node and sub-task pairs.
evidence.support_explanation: Write rule: store on (LLM-declared) completion; no separate executable or outcome gate.

evidence.quote: When learning a new sub-task, MobileGPT stores actions in a generalized format to ensure that they are reusable across different contexts.
evidence.support_explanation: Stored actions are de-instantiated (UI attributes and task parameters replaced by placeholders).

evidence.quote: Specifically, the example includes a prior user instruction, an abbreviated version of the past screen representation, and its correct output.
evidence.support_explanation: When attribute-based adaptation fails, a stored correct example is used as a one-shot conditioning prompt.

evidence.quote: In case self-correction falls short, MobileGPT provides mechanisms for users to correct the LLM’s mistakes themselves.
evidence.support_explanation: Human repairs are written into the stored path.

evidence.quote: we have heuristically identified two main types of commonly occurring errors and developed a rule-based self-feedback generation module.
evidence.support_explanation: Rule-based, within-episode feedback (invalid UI index, no screen change, loops); not itself retained.

evidence.quote: A task was considered successful if the system navigated to the final screen within these three attempts.
evidence.support_explanation: Success = reaching the final screen with up to three extra self-correction attempts (lenient, arrival-based).

evidence.quote: To ensure a fair evaluation in the comparison study, we did not utilize
evidence.support_explanation: Table 1 comparison excludes the HITL repair feature (sentence continues: MobileGPT's HITL task repair feature).

evidence.quote: had one additional failure than its cold-start due to an error while recalling a task from memory.
evidence.support_explanation: Autonomous warm-start (82.16%) is not better than cold-start (82.7%): memory does not raise accuracy without human repair.

evidence.quote: If it fails to correct itself, we mark the task as a failure and manually repair the error using the HITL task repair.
evidence.support_explanation: Ablation study (source of 98.75%) lets the authors repair failures and store the repaired path.

evidence.quote: This improvement over the cold-start accuracy is due to the user’s ability to correct task executions before saving them to memory
evidence.support_explanation: Authors attribute the cold-to-warm accuracy rise to human correction before saving, not autonomous learning.

evidence.quote: This baseline is designed to share the same prompts as MobileGPT while following the traditional Derive-only structure employed in prior approaches
evidence.support_explanation: Same-prompt, Derive-only baseline isolates structure+memory from prompt wording.

evidence.quote: dramatically reduces latency and cost, achieving improvements of 62.5% and 68.8% over the baseline, respectively.
evidence.support_explanation: Warm-start (same high-level task, new parameters) efficiency gain; author report on 80 tasks of the authors' dataset.

evidence.quote: The main contribution of MobileGPT lies in improving performance for repeated tasks and sub-tasks.
evidence.support_explanation: Evaluation set was built by the authors to exhibit repetition; the claimed benefit is efficiency on repeated tasks.

evidence.quote: Each task is accompanied by two user instructions with different task parameters—totaling 160 user instructions
evidence.support_explanation: Warm-start test instance is a sibling instruction of the cold-start instance used to build the memory.

evidence.quote: The cold-start executes the first instruction set from each high-level task, and the warm-start executes the second instruction set.
evidence.support_explanation: Construction (cold) and test (warm) streams share the high-level task; reuse is by design, cross-task transfer is not tested for accuracy.

evidence.quote: Notably, when MobileGPT makes an error during a subtask and receives a correction, either through self-feedback generation or HTIL task repair, it avoids repeating the same mistake in other tasks involving overlapping subtasks.
evidence.support_explanation: Evidence of sub-task-level reuse across tasks (qualitative example: Telegram contact search).

evidence.quote: Conversely, Gmail shows a low memory hit rate (6.7%), as its tasks have few overlapping sub-tasks.
evidence.support_explanation: Memory benefit depends on overlap; memory hit rates reported per app (Table 3).

evidence.quote: In our evaluation, out of 327 primitive actions, 53 actions (16.2%) were not adaptable through attribute-based adaptation and therefore required in-context adaptation via LLM.
evidence.support_explanation: Fallback path frequency; all 53 adapted correctly according to authors.

evidence.quote: with Mann-Whitney U Test results of
evidence.support_explanation: Only statistical tests in the paper are for the 23-participant usability study, not for task success.

evidence.quote: These app pages accounted for 89.65% (104 out of 116) of the total app pages required during the evaluation.
evidence.support_explanation: Memory is pre-populated by random exploration of the evaluation apps; page coverage of the test apps is high.

evidence.quote: The total cost for this random exploration was $10.78, which is deemed reasonable considering that this preparation is a one-time process.
evidence.support_explanation: Construction cost for offline exploration is reported.

evidence.quote: At the time of evaluation, the LLM costs (per 1K tokens) were: GPT-4-Turbo $0.01, GPT-3.5 Turbo $0.003
evidence.support_explanation: Cost computed from token prices.

evidence.quote: Comparisons were made only for tasks successfully completed by all three systems (77 tasks).
evidence.support_explanation: Cost/latency comparison in Sec 7.2 uses 77 of 185 tasks (successes only).

evidence.quote: The step accuracy of the baseline is 92.4%
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline step accuracy; MobileGPT cold 95.5%, warm 99.8% (Table 2).

evidence.quote: The current implementation of MobileGPT does not support mobile apps that lack text representation of their screen layouts
evidence.support_explanation: Stated applicability boundary.

evidence.quote: We manually monitored each step to identify errors during task execution.
evidence.support_explanation: Success labelling is manual by the authors; annotator count and agreement not reported.
Overall success: AutoDroid 74.7%, AppAgent 67.4%, MobileGPT cold 82.7%, warm 82.16% (185 tasks, 18 apps, no HITL).

evidence.quote: In our evaluation, where MobileGPT encountered and classified 269 app screens, this method showed only 3 false positives (misclassifying different app pages as the same node) and no false negatives
evidence.support_explanation: Screen classification by sub-task requirements vs two baseline classifiers (38/57 false positives).

evidence.quote: The output in the example could either be an action originally generated by the LLM during the Derive phase or one that has been modified by the user through the HITL task repair.
evidence.support_explanation: Stored examples can be human-written, so the library partly grows through supervision.

evidence.quote: Third, UIs may change unexpectedly with app updates.
evidence.support_explanation: Staleness is handled by LLM re-derivation fallback; no versioning or invalidation described.

evidence.quote: To the best of our knowledge, MobileGPT is the first to explore caching within the context of an LLM-based task automator.
evidence.support_explanation: Author novelty claim; AutoDroid's exploration-built app knowledge is described but not compared as memory.

evidence.quote: However, LLMs are inherently non-deterministic.
evidence.support_explanation: Nondeterminism acknowledged; no repeated runs or variance reported for success rates.

evidence.quote: We observed that tasks that would take just over 30 seconds for a human could take more than two minutes for an LLM, and cost over a dollar each time they are performed.
evidence.support_explanation: Anecdotal motivation for the cost/latency gap.

signatures.object: Per-app hierarchical memory: page nodes (defined by their sub-task lists), sub-task edges (parameterised action sequences), tasks (sequences of node/sub-task pairs)
signatures.information: Simplified HTML screen representation, user instruction, LLM outputs of Explore/Select/Derive (GPT-4-turbo) and slot-filling (GPT-3.5); offline random-explorer and trace-monitor screens; no outcome oracle
signatures.operation: Explore->Select->Derive on a cache miss; store the completed task; Recall replays the stored sub-task sequence with slot-filling, attribute-based action adaptation, and a one-shot in-context adaptation fallback
signatures.output: Reusable task/sub-task/action records with generalised UI attributes and parameter placeholders
signatures.conditions: Android apps with text-extractable layouts; repeated tasks and overlapping sub-tasks
signatures.feedback: Execution errors (invalid index, no screen change, loops) and optional human repair
signatures.selection_rule: Store when Select returns Finish; node dedup by sub-task requirements plus cosine similarity; no measured admission test
signatures.persistence: Server-side per-app graph reused across sessions
signatures.later_use: Instruction -> high-level task match -> memory replay, sub-task reuse in other tasks, few-shot example on fallback
signatures.claimed_effect: Warm-start latency -62.5%, cost -68.8% vs same-prompt Derive-only baseline; cold-start success 82.7% vs AutoDroid 74.7 / AppAgent 67.4
signatures.failure_boundary: UI changes, ambiguous attributes, image-only screens (Flutter/web/maps), crucial irreversible actions during repair

signatures.object: Executed path corrected by rule-based self-feedback or a human, then written to memory
signatures.information: Rule-detected error messages appended to next prompt; human edits sub-task list, selected sub-task/parameters, or demonstrated actions
signatures.operation: Within-episode self-correction (not retained) and human repair (retained in the stored path / example)
signatures.output: Repaired task path stored for recall

gap.author_gap: LLM task automators are unreliable (non-deterministic) and costly in time and money on repeated tasks; demonstration/macro approaches need human demos or fail to generalise actions.
gap.checked_gap: Real and measurable for repetitive mobile tasks (cost/latency, repeat-run variability); the paper's own accuracy results show memory lowers cost rather than improving autonomous accuracy.
gap.lineage: API assistants / programming-by-demonstration -> LLM agents without memory (AutoDroid, AppAgent) -> LLM agent with sub-task-level reusable memory; macro mining (Li & Riva, Toyama random explorer, Huang et al.)
gap.closest_adjacent: AutoDroid and AppAgent (empirical baselines), macro-mining work (discussed), LLM response caching; agent-memory work such as ExpeL/Voyager-style stores is not discussed
gap.residue: Repeated-task cost and latency; error repetition across overlapping sub-tasks
gap.stakes: Over two minutes and about one dollar per task as stated anecdotally
gap.method_response: Sub-task-level memory with parameter generalisation, adaptive recall and human repair
gap.remaining_gap: No autonomous accuracy gain from memory, no invalidation under UI change, generalisation to unseen task types untested, Android text-layout only
unresolved: AutoDroid's exploration-derived app knowledge and generic agent-memory neighbours are not available in the pinned materials; novelty of 'first caching' is taken from the authors.
